specStatements.text: Plant diseases can be detected by: stunted growth; spots on leaves; areas of decay (rot); growths; malformed stems or leaves; discolouration; the presence of pests.
Identification can be made by: reference to a gardening manual or website; taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen; using testing kits that contain monoclonal antibodies.
Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as well as by insects.
Knowledge of plant diseases is restricted to tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects.
Plants can be damaged by a range of ion deficiency conditions: stunted growth caused by nitrate deficiency; chlorosis caused by magnesium deficiency.
Knowledge of ions is limited to nitrate ions needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, and magnesium ions needed to make chlorophyll.
Students should be able to describe physical and chemical plant defence responses.
Physical defence responses to resist invasion of microorganisms. Cellulose cell walls.; Tough waxy cuticle on leaves.; Layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees) which fall off.
Chemical plant defence responses. Antibacterial chemicals.; Poisons to deter herbivores.
Mechanical adaptations. Thorns and hairs deter animals.; Leaves which droop or curl when touched.; Mimicry to trick animals.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Knowledge of plant diseases is kept to the three named examples only: tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects. No other plant disease is named anywhere in the concepts, misconceptions or questions, and no named example of a bacterial plant disease is given, even though bacterial pathogens are mentioned as a category.

Knowledge of ions is kept to nitrate ions, needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, and magnesium ions, needed to make chlorophyll. No other mineral ions are named, and no detail of how ions are absorbed by roots, or of fertiliser composition, is included.

concepts.definition: Plant diseases can be detected from observable signs on the plant: stunted growth, spots on leaves, areas of decay (rot), growths, malformed stems or leaves, discolouration, and the presence of pests.

Once a disease has been detected, it can be identified by reference to a gardening manual or website, by taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen, or by using testing kits that contain monoclonal antibodies.

A viral pathogen of plants. It gives a distinctive mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves; because the discoloured areas contain less chlorophyll, less photosynthesis occurs and the growth of the plant is affected.
A fungal disease of roses. Purple or black spots develop on the leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early, so less photosynthesis occurs and the growth of the plant is affected.
Insects that infest plants and feed on them, taking dissolved sugars and other nutrients from the plant and so weakening it. Aphids are insects, not pathogens.
Nitrate ions are needed by a plant for protein synthesis and therefore for growth. A plant grown in soil short of nitrate ions shows stunted growth.
Magnesium ions are needed by a plant to make chlorophyll. A plant short of magnesium ions cannot make enough chlorophyll and shows chlorosis, in which the leaves turn yellow.
Structures that resist invasion of microorganisms: cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle on leaves, and layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees) which fall off.
Substances a plant produces to defend itself: antibacterial chemicals, and poisons to deter herbivores.
Adaptations that protect a plant from animals: thorns and hairs which deter animals, leaves which droop or curl when touched, and mimicry to trick animals.

misconceptions.question: A plant's leaves have turned yellow. Which ion deficiency causes this?
misconceptions.correct: A magnesium deficiency. Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, and a shortage causes chlorosis.
misconceptions.misconception: Yellow leaves show that a plant is short of nitrate ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nitrate is the ion students meet most often, and they associate it with healthy green plants, so any loss of leaf colour is blamed on it.
misconceptions.correction: Knowledge of ions is limited to nitrate ions needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, and magnesium ions needed to make chlorophyll. Nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth; magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis.

misconceptions.question: A plant is discoloured and growing poorly. Does this prove a pathogen has infected it?
misconceptions.correct: No. Plants can also be damaged by ion deficiency conditions, so the same signs can be produced without any pathogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Any damage, discolouration, growth or poor growth seen on a plant means a pathogen has infected it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The signs used to detect disease, such as stunted growth and discolouration, are learned as a list of disease signs, so students read every sign as proof of infection.
misconceptions.correction: Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as well as by insects, but plants can also be damaged by a range of ion deficiency conditions: stunted growth caused by nitrate deficiency; chlorosis caused by magnesium deficiency.

misconceptions.question: Aphids damage plants. Are aphids pathogens?
misconceptions.correct: No. Aphids are insects, which damage plants by feeding on them rather than by infecting them as a pathogen does.
misconceptions.misconception: Aphids are microorganisms that infect plants in the same way as bacteria and fungi do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Aphids are listed alongside viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as a cause of plant damage, so students assume they must be another kind of microorganism.
misconceptions.correction: Plants can be infected by a range of viral, bacterial and fungal pathogens as well as by insects. Knowledge of plant diseases is restricted to tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects.

misconceptions.question: Are thorns, hairs and leaves that curl when touched physical defence responses?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are mechanical adaptations, which deter or trick animals rather than resist invasion of microorganisms.
misconceptions.misconception: Thorns, hairs and leaves that droop or curl are physical defences that stop microorganisms getting into the plant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Thorns and hairs are physical structures you can see and touch, so students file them under 'physical defence' without asking what they act against.
misconceptions.correction: Physical defence responses resist invasion of microorganisms: cellulose cell walls; tough waxy cuticle on leaves; layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees) which fall off. Thorns and hairs which deter animals, and leaves which droop or curl when touched, are mechanical adaptations.

misconceptions.question: A plant makes antibacterial chemicals. Is that a physical defence response?
misconceptions.correct: No. Antibacterial chemicals, and poisons to deter herbivores, are chemical plant defence responses.
misconceptions.misconception: Antibacterial chemicals and poisons count as physical defences because they sit on or inside the plant's tissues.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat anything that forms part of the plant body as 'physical', instead of separating defences by whether the plant makes a substance or has a structure.
misconceptions.correction: Chemical plant defence responses are antibacterial chemicals and poisons to deter herbivores. Physical defence responses are cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle on leaves, and layers of dead cells around stems which fall off.

misconceptions.question: Which type of pathogen causes black spot, and which causes tobacco mosaic virus disease?
misconceptions.correct: Black spot is a fungal disease; tobacco mosaic virus is a viral disease.
misconceptions.misconception: Black spot is a viral disease and tobacco mosaic virus is a fungal disease.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both diseases are met at the same time and both are seen as discoloured marks on leaves, so students swap the two named examples over.
misconceptions.correction: Knowledge of plant diseases is restricted to tobacco mosaic virus as a viral disease, black spot as a fungal disease and aphids as insects.

mcqs.stem: A plant has grown to the normal height for its age, but its leaves have turned yellow. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A lack of nitrate ions, needed to make chlorophyll
options.rationale: A student who links yellow leaves to nitrate picks this. Nitrate ions are needed for protein synthesis and therefore growth, not for chlorophyll, and a nitrate deficiency causes stunted growth rather than yellowing.

options.text: A lack of magnesium ions, needed to make chlorophyll
options.rationale: Magnesium ions are needed to make chlorophyll, so a magnesium deficiency causes chlorosis, in which the leaves turn yellow while height can stay normal.

options.text: An infection by black spot, a fungal plant disease
options.rationale: A student who believes every sign on a plant means infection reaches for a named pathogen. Black spot produces purple or black spots on rose leaves; general yellowing with normal growth points to an ion deficiency condition instead.

options.text: An attack by aphids, which are plant microorganisms
options.rationale: A student who thinks aphids are microorganisms that infect plants chooses this. Aphids are insects, they would be visible on the plant as pests, and they are not the cause of chlorosis.

mcqs.stem: Which of these plant problems is caused by a fungal pathogen?

options.text: Black spot, giving dark marks on rose leaves
options.rationale: Black spot is the named fungal disease of plants: purple or black spots develop on the leaves, which often turn yellow and drop early.

options.text: Aphid infestation, giving reduced plant growth
options.rationale: A student who treats aphids as a kind of microorganism counts them as a pathogen. Aphids are insects, so they are pests that feed on the plant, not fungal pathogens.

options.text: Chlorosis, giving yellow patches on leaves
options.rationale: A student who reads every sign of damage as infection picks this. Chlorosis is an ion deficiency condition caused by a lack of magnesium ions, so no pathogen is involved.

options.text: Tobacco mosaic virus, giving a mosaic pattern
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the two named diseases over labels this one fungal. Tobacco mosaic virus is the named viral disease; it gives a mosaic pattern of discolouration on the leaves.

mcqs.stem: A rose plant has sharp thorns on its stems. Which type of plant defence is this?

options.text: A physical defence that resists microorganisms
options.rationale: A student who groups all visible structures as physical defences picks this. Physical defence responses resist invasion of microorganisms and are cellulose cell walls, a tough waxy cuticle and layers of dead cells around stems.

options.text: A chemical defence that kills invading bacteria
options.rationale: A student who has not separated substances the plant makes from structures it grows picks this. Chemical plant defence responses are antibacterial chemicals and poisons; a thorn is not a chemical.

options.text: A sign of infection by a fungal plant pathogen
options.rationale: A student who reads any unusual structure as a disease sign treats a thorn as a growth caused by infection. Thorns are a normal adaptation of the plant, not a sign of a fungal pathogen.

options.text: A mechanical adaptation that deters animals
options.rationale: Thorns and hairs deter animals, so they are listed as mechanical adaptations rather than as physical or chemical defence responses.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a physical defence response that resists invasion of microorganisms?

options.text: Poisons which are made in the leaves
options.rationale: A student who counts anything held inside the plant as physical picks this. Poisons to deter herbivores are a chemical plant defence response.

options.text: Hairs which grow on the leaf surfaces
options.rationale: A student who groups visible structures with the physical defences picks this. Hairs deter animals, so they are a mechanical adaptation, not a defence against microorganisms.

options.text: Leaves which curl when they are touched
options.rationale: The same belief leads a student to treat a touch response as a barrier. Leaves which droop or curl when touched are a mechanical adaptation that acts against animals, not against microorganisms.

options.text: Layers of dead cells around the stems
options.rationale: Layers of dead cells around stems (bark on trees), which fall off, are a physical defence response that resists invasion of microorganisms.

mcqs.stem: A grower sees stunted growth and discoloured leaves on a crop, and a gardening website does not settle what is wrong. What should be done next to identify the cause?

options.text: Add nitrate fertiliser to the soil to restore leaf colour
options.rationale: A student who blames discoloured leaves on nitrate jumps straight to treatment. Chlorosis is caused by magnesium deficiency, and adding fertiliser identifies nothing.

options.text: Spray the whole crop with a fungicide to kill black spot
options.rationale: A student who assumes any sign means infection treats before identifying. The signs could come from an ion deficiency condition, and spraying does not identify the cause.

options.text: Take the plant to a laboratory to identify the pathogen
options.rationale: Identification can be made by taking infected plants to a laboratory to identify the pathogen, which is the step to take when a gardening manual or website is not enough.

options.text: Look for a mosaic pattern to confirm a fungal disease
options.rationale: A student who has swapped the named diseases expects a mosaic pattern to show a fungus. A mosaic pattern of discolouration indicates tobacco mosaic virus, a viral disease, and this crop shows no such pattern.
